title: Advanced approach for target small RNAs enrichment from biological samples and sequencing library preparation (TSR-Seq)
text:
Small RNAs and RNA fragments (sRNAs) derived from cell-free RNA and found in circulation are emerging as a
novel class of biomarkers for detecting cancer at early stages and posttreatment with higher sensitivity in
comparison to circulating tumor-derived DNAs. Transcription in multiple copies of tumor-associated RNA from
corresponding DNA, dysregulated post-transcriptional events, formation of chimeric RNAs, and high level of
cfRNA fragmentation contribute to the sRNA higher abundance, complexity, and cancer specificity. The goal of
this project is to develop the most advanced research and diagnostic method of sequencing library preparation,
providing highly sensitive and specific detection of sRNAs of interest (target sRNAs) in human plasma.

title: Dual targeting chemokine receptors prevents chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity
text:
The objective of this study is to validate an innovative concept that the unique dual TC14012 protects against
doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity (DICT) by activating cardiac CXCR7 to reprogram cardiomyocyte
metabolism and prevent cardiac dysfunction and by antagonizing CXCR4 to inhibit cardiac mast cell infiltration
and activation in multiple mouse models. We will first optimize the doses of TC14012 for protecting against
DICT in two tumor-free and tumor-bearing mouse models, and then we will determine its direct effects and
mechanisms on energy reserve metabolism and mitochondrial function in cardiomyocytes and on cardiac mast
cell infiltration and degranulation. This project will reveal new insight into the underlying mechanisms behind
and provide fundamental evidence for TC14012 as a novel approach for the prevention of DICT in future
clinical studies.

title: Investigating the role of the RNA helicase F57B9.3 in translational regulation under conditions of lipid depletion
text:
Previous studies have shed light on how nutrient deprivation, such as glucose and amino acids, affect translation.
My investigation into the regulatory mechanism of translation following lipid depletion suggests it is distinct from
those activated during glucose and amino acid depletion with the RNA helicase, F57B9.3 (C. elegans ortholog
of eukaryotic initiation factor 4A) playing a crucial role. Therefore, the research proposed in this fellowship has
potential to broaden our current understanding of translational regulation and the completion of the aims
proposed herein will characterize the role of F57B9.3 while elucidating the molecular mechanism underlying
lipid-depletion induced changes in translation.

title: Minnesota Dental, Oral and Craniofacial Training in Research
text:
Oral diseases impact over 3.5 billion people globally, posing a significant challenge to public health. To
address this burden, it is vital to train the next generation of oral and craniofacial biologists and clinician
scientists to develop treatments to enhance overall health and improve patients' quality of life. This training
program is designed to equip trainees with comprehensive knowledge of oral diseases while fostering a
lifelong commitment to uncovering the underlying biological mechanisms that drive these conditions.

title: Epithelial Reprogramming Underpinning Euplastic versus Dysplastic Repair
text:
Chronic lung diseases like idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), with no viable cure or effective therapies, are
characterized by regenerative failure of the stem cells. Understanding how these stem cells, usually adept
promoting regeneration, fail in these diseases can lead to development of therapeutics. Therefore, this
proposal aims to understand the mechanisms underlying how lung epithelial stem cells undergo a pathogenic
and dysplastic regenerative processes instead of injury-resolving, euplastic regenerative processes.

title: SUNBEAM2 Gap Supplement
text:
Atopic dermatitis (AD) and food allergy are among the most common chronic diseases of early childhood. These
diseases often occur in the same individuals and many times lead to the development of hay fever and asthma,
in a poorly understood process termed the allergic march. In this project we will investigate whether early-life
barrier and immune abnormalities of the skin result in not only AD, but affect the overall immune system, leading
to the allergic march.

title: Mechanical signaling through the nuclear membrane in lung alveolar health
text:
The mammalian respiratory system undergoes cyclical mechanical strain as part of its normal function. We
hypothesize that the lung has evolved specific epigenetic and transcriptional mechanisms to maintain cellular
fate in the face of mechanical strain from normal respiration and these pathways are altered in the response to
injury and disease. In this proposal, we aim to address key unanswered questions in cell fate regulation in lung
development and regeneration.

title: Platinum-induced lipid reprogramming and tumor immune microenvironment in SCLC
text:
Dendritic cells are professional antigen-presenting cells and play a pivotal role in antitumor immunity and
effective immunotherapy. We found that platinum-based chemotherapy reprograms lipid metabolism in small cell
lung cancer, which reshapes the function of dendritic cells and leads to immune evasion. In this proposal, we will
uncover the molecular mechanism by which platinum induces lipid reprograming and validate PPARa signaling
as a therapeutic target to improve platinum/immunotherapy combination in small cell lung cancer.

title: The role of Smyd4 in regulating cardioprogenitor specification.
text: Members of SET and MYND domain-containing protein (SMYDs) family are unique lysine methyltransferases that play important roles during embryogenesis via the regulation of histone H3 lysine residues that impart both transcriptional activation and repression functions. SMYD1 is known for its function in regulating cardiomyocyte differentiation and maturation. Our previous study on the role of SMYD4 in Zebrafish suggesting that smyd4 is critical to early embryonic development and cardiogenesis. Our recent transcriptomic analysis of smyd4-ablated zebrafish blastula and early gastrula embryos has revealed significant changes in gene regulatory networks involved in the specification of mesendoderm and the differentiation of cardiac progenitor cells (CPCs). These data suggest that smyd4 may be involved in cardiogenic-lineage specification and differentiation prior to overt heart formation. Importantly, we demonstrate that de novo SMYD4 genetic variants are associated with congenital heart defects (CHDs). To establish the mechanistic basis for the genetic association of SMYD4 to CHDs, we have analyzed the temporal expression pattern of SMYD4 within human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and their induced differentiation into cardiomyocytes. We find that SMYD4 is expressed throughout the differentiation process from hESCs to cardiomyocytes. Genetic ablation of SMYD4 in hESCs (hESC-SMYD4KO) resulted in dramatically compromised mesodermal specification and CPC differentiation, thus phenocopying the early developmental and cardiac defects observed in smyd4 mutant zebrafish. Additional transcriptomic analysis further supports that induced cardiomyogenic differentiation of hESCs-SMYD4KO is severely altered, where hESCs-SMYD4KO adopt a more neuroectodermal lineage fate. Quantitative mass spectrometry analysis reveals that BACH1, a critical transcriptional regulator of stem cell pluripotency and lineage specification, as a strong SMYD4 binding partner. Based on these preliminary data, we hypothesize that SMYD4 functions as a critical epigenetic regulator for mesendoderm specification and cardiac development via its interaction with BACH1. In this project, we propose 3 specific aims to define the biological and molecular function of SMYD4 in mesendoderm specification and cardiac development. Aim 1 tests the hypothesis that SMYD4 is critical to mesoderm specification and cardiogenic differentiation by performing genetic rescue experiment and a series of genome-wide integrated analyses, including the single-cell RNA-seq and DNA occupancy analyses, to define the potentially altered histone epigenetic landscape during cardiomyocyte differentiation in mutant hESCs. Aim 2 tests the hypothesis that BACH1-SMYD4 complexes are critical to the epigenetic regulation of mesoderm specification and cardiogenic differentiation by determining the protein-protein interaction domains and BACH1- SMYD4 specific targeted genes using CUT&RUN analysis. Aim 3 tests the hypothesis that SMYD4 is essential to mammalian cardiac development by the generation and characterization of SMYD4 mutant mouse lines.

title: Micro-nanotechnologies for the analysis of islet-derived extracellular vesicles implicated in Type 1 Diabetes
text:
Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) are shed by all cells in the body into the blood, and so provide a unique opportunity
for monitoring the pancreatic islet microenvironment with liquid biopsies. Here we propose to integrate an
innovative tool set of bulk and single EV omics, nanotechnologies, and microtechnologies to extract the blood
fingerprints of Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) and to develop EV based biomarkers for the early detection of T1D. The
proposed methodology, as well as data set, will be of high value to the fundamental and clinical T1D
communities.

title: Trauma, the gut, and the brain: the gut microbiota-microglia axis in traumatic brain injury
text:
Traumatic brain injury afflicts approximately three million Americans every year with a high rate of long-term
cognitive and psychiatric morbidity. Chronic neuroinflammation resulting from the constitutive activation of
microglia is complicit in this process and represents a complex interplay between the injured brain, microglia,
and the gut microbiome via the gut-brain axis. However, the mechanism(s) underlying gut microbiota-microglia
interaction have yet to be elucidated.

title: Theraputic targeting of pulmonary endothelial cells to inhibit pathological lung remodeling
text:
Project Narrative.
We propose to develop the new therapeutic approaches to restore microvascular integrity during lung
fibrogenesis with the goal to decrease the disease progression. We will use newly developed lung
EC-specific nanoparticles and transplantation with donor FOXF1+cKIT+ endothelial progenitor cells to
improve lung microvascular integrity and prevent fibrotic lung remodeling. The outcomes from our
studies are expected to have an important positive impact on human health because of the high
translational potential of the proposed new therapies in IPF.

title: Discovering regulators of tissue mechanics driving vertebrate morphogenesis
text:
Understanding how organs form in a developing embryo will advance treatment of devastating birth defects
and provide a roadmap for regenerative strategies to grow new organs to replace those compromised during
adulthood. Organogenesis requires coordination of biochemical and mechanical processes, so that precise
forces can be generated on tissues of finely regulated physical properties to stereotypically produce target
morphologies during normal development. The present application focuses on intestinal development to
discover new genes and signaling pathways that regulate tissue mechanics during embryonic development,
expanding the molecular-mechanical toolbox available for engineering complex functional tissues in the future.

title: Protein assemblies as genetically encoded mechanical actuators for intracellular mechanobiology research
text:
The fast-progressing field of mechanobiology has unveiled the key regulatory roles of mechanical forces in
biology and advanced our understandings of pathogeneses in numerous disorders. However, the available
tools exhibit limited capabilities for precise intracellular mechanical perturbation at cellular/subcellular levels.
We will fill the technological gap with a series of genetically encoded in-cellulo mechanical actuators that
exhibit precise, multimodal, and high-throughput force exertion and offer a clear pathway towards in-vivo
studies, thus facilitating the mechanistic studies in mechanotransduction and helping solve the associated
puzzles in pathology.

title: Understanding Lrig1+ in vocal fold epithelium and organoid biology
text:
Vocal fold (VF) inflammatory lesions are common voice disorders related to disrupted epithelial homeostasis
accompanied by inflammatory infiltrates and changes in the lamina propria. These lesions cause notable
changes in voicing thereby impacting the quality of life. In this application, we seek to provide comprehensive
characterization of VF Lrig1+ cells as a population of epithelial stem cells that are responsible for hyperplastic
epithelial changes associated with disease condition and generate organoids as a reliable culture system to
understand VF epithelium health and disease.

title: Improving Perception in Digital Breast Tomography
text:
8. PROJECT NARRATIVE
Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) is a technology that improves breast cancer screening accuracy over
classic mammography but its large number of images means that it takes more time to read. We will
investigate a series of interventions that can improve the speed and/or accuracy of DBT cancer screening.
What we learn will advance our fundamental understandingof visual search and will be useful in any setting
where technology has produced more images than users have time to examine.

title: The transcription factor basonuclin-1, a new player in the progression of triple-negative inflammatory breast cancer
text: Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC) is a highly aggressive and lethal form of breast cancer. The proposed research aims to advance our understanding of the molecular signaling pathways involved in IBC, enabling the evaluation of BNC-1 as a potential biomarker and the identification of novel, targeted therapeutic strategies to improve patient outcomes.

title: Biostatistics & Data Management Core
text: ABSTRACT, Biostatistics and Data Management Core (BDMC) The Biostatistics and Data Management Core (BDMC) plays a critical role in the success of cancer research at the Indiana University Simon Comprehensive Cancer Center (IUSCCC) by providing state-of-the-art biostatistical and data science support and data management services. This includes the design, conduct, analysis, and interpretation of clinical trials, basic science experimental studies, population-based research, and studies using real-world data. For clinical trials initiated by IUSCCC members, the BDMC provides biostatistics and data management support for trials conducted by the IUSCCC Clinical Trials Office and biostatistics support for trials conducted by the Hoosier Cancer Research Network and Big Ten Cancer Research Network. The BDMC is comprised of faculty and staff biostatisticians, data scientists, and data managers. This Shared Resource collaborates with members of all IUSCCC Research Programs. The primary mission of BDMC is to facilitate cancer research for IUSCCC members, especially by assisting them with obtaining peer-reviewed federal grants and journal publications. The BDMC also contributes substantially to education and training (e.g., mentoring residents, fellows, and junior investigators) and scientific review (e.g., IUSCCC Scientific Review Committee). Since the last competitive renewal, the BDMC has fulfilled its stated plans to prepare for IUSCCC growth by increasing the number and expertise of faculty and staff; increasing cross-core collaborations with the Cancer Bioinformatics Core (CBC) when developing grant proposals that involve both bioinformatics and biostatistics; implementing novel statistical designs for genomic-guided clinical trials; and augmenting statistical expertise for analyzing high-throughput “omics” data. Specific initiatives achieved in the current grant period to meet the increasing and specialized research activities at IUSCCC include substantially increasing the BDMC faculty effort; creating a new area called Real World Data; creating a co-Director role to complement the expertise of the Director; creating new Associate Director roles, which grow leadership and optimize triaging of requests according to expertise; expanding expertise in data science, machine learning, basic science, and clinical trials; and creating and filling a new cross-core Program Manager position to strengthen coordination with the CBC while facilitating communication with IUSCCC members and internal and external partners. When necessary, high-impact statistical methodologies are developed to address scientific problems arising from cancer studies. Plans for the next five-year cycle include growing our expertise in all four areas of cancer research (basic science, clinical trials, population science, and real-world data); broadening our data science expertise in all position levels; increasing the frequency with which we apply novel methods to published cancer collaborations; and extending our successful coordination with the CBC to include integration of cancer-related data science silos throughout our campus.

title: Nanopore technology development for reading intact proteoforms
text:
We are developing a next-generation platform for single-molecule, full-length protein analysis
that directly reads intact proteoforms and post-translational modifications using
unfoldase-coupled nanopore arrays. By integrating new molecular strategies, large-scale
barcoded proteoform libraries, advanced machine learning analysis, and validation on BRCA1
with co-investigator Dr. Tom Walsh and collaborator Dr. Mary-Claire King, we will advance this
technology from proof-of-concept toward a broadly useful prototype. Our long-term partnership
with Oxford Nanopore provides access to cutting-edge platforms and translational expertise,
positioning this platform to transform proteomics and accelerate biomedical discovery.

title: Biology and Biotechnology of Cell and Gene Therapy
text: Cell and gene therapy – including gene therapy for rare or complex disease, genome editing, cell replacement, and tissue engineering – are emerging as the next generation of therapeutics to address unmet medical needs. Their investigation is also enabling basic investigation of human development and modeling of human disease. Scientists with interdisciplinary backgrounds in biology and engineering are needed to rapidly advance these fields. To address this need, the primary objective of this Biology and Biotechnology of Cell and Gene Therapy Training Program is to provide structured and supportive interdisciplinary classroom and research training opportunities in these rapidly evolving and expanding disciplines.
